whyThisMatters: Real Technology Team moments are fast — a ticket, a call, an alert, a PR, a dependency, a CI notification — and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits across the full range of what the job throws at you, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a plausible ticket number, a familiar tool's look, a caller who won't wait, a package with the right name, a PR comment that reads like a real review. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. With the combined pool now covering both help-desk and development scenarios, most people get at least one from the "other side" wrong on their first try.
Ask why asking a caller for a ticket reference number, or a contributor for more details, doesn't actually verify anything in either case.
Ask why taking extra time despite pressure is listed as a good habit, even when it feels like it's making someone else's problem worse.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to verify a request that already looks like a normal part of their job.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like part of the job — a plausible ticket number, a tool's familiar look, an urgent caller, a package with a reasonable name, a PR comment styled like a real review — without checking the actual sending domain, console, or publish history. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit, on either side of the combined set.

bubbles.note: An attacker can invent any reference number that sounds plausible — asking for one feels like a check but doesn't verify anything on its own.

bubbles.text: Rotated A Password On The Normal Schedule
bubbles.note: Scheduled rotation is good hygiene, but an exposed credential can't wait for the next cycle — exposure means instant rotation, not queued rotation.
